# Why TPMS Alerts Trigger After Tire Replacement

When a Tire Pressure Monitoring System (TPMS) warning light illuminates after a tire change, it is rarely a hardware failure and almost never a recalibration issue regarding wheel spin speed. The root cause lies in how modern vehicles detect pressure versus how the service technician approached the maintenance window.

Most 2015 Honda CRVs, like many vehicles from that era, utilize direct TPMS sensors embedded within the valve stems of each tire. These are not indirect systems that infer pressure by analyzing wheel rotation variance during braking or coasting. As demonstrated in your scenario where the alert triggered while stopped at a traffic light with no braking involved, an indirect system relies entirely on ABS data to detect relative speed differences between wheels. Since your car lit up without motion, the sensor inside the tire is broadcasting a "low pressure" or "missing sensor" signal directly to the ECU (Engine Control Unit).

The most common technical reason for this specific failure mode is that the new tires were not yet mounted when the sensors were installed, or the mounting process damaged the sensor. If the shop installed the sensor before inflating the tire to full pressure, or if they failed to use a dedicated TPMS extension valve tool during inflation, the high pressure of the bead seating can shear the delicate stem seal. This is a mechanical failure of the interface between the rubber and the metal sensor. Additionally, many sensors have a finite battery life (typically 5–10 years). If your vehicle has seen multiple tire rotations over that decade, it is highly probable one or more sensors simply died coincidentally with the tire replacement, rather than being broken by the shop.

From a debugging perspective, you should treat this like troubleshooting a network connectivity issue: verify the signal source first. In many Honda models, turning the ignition to the "ON" position without starting the engine allows you to listen for a rhythmic clicking sound coming from each wheel. This is the sensor transmitting its ID to the central control module. If one wheel is silent while others click, that specific sensor has lost communication power or its antenna ring is obstructed by a non-standard valve cap.

Standard OBD-II scanners often fail here because they query for pressure values rather than raw sensor IDs. You need a TPMS-specific diagnostic tool to see if the ECU sees "Low Pressure" (indicating actual air loss) or "No Signal" (indicating the battery is dead or the stem was sheared). If the shop claims they don't have mechanics and refuses to inspect, ask them specifically if they used a valve core removal tool that includes an integrated antenna shield. Cheap tools often strip these shields off, rendering the sensor invisible to the car's receiver even if it has air in it.

The solution usually involves one of two paths: replacing the dead sensors (often requiring reprogramming to the vehicle's VIN) or repairing the specific stem connection. Do not rely on resetting the light via the dashboard menu; that only clears the error code temporarily without fixing the underlying transmission issue. If the sensor is truly gone, the system will remain in a fault loop until the hardware is replaced and synced.

For developers thinking of building similar systems, remember that edge cases like mechanical interference during installation are often more frequent than software bugs. Robust systems require telemetry at the physical interface level, not just high-level data interpretation.
